overview.title: Target mask and loading the dataset into memory
overview.section: 11.2 Training a segmentation model from scratch
overview.main_topic: Figure 11.4 (the trimap for the example cat) and helper functions that shuffle, resize and convert images and masks for in-memory loading
overview.central_idea: Because the Pets dataset is small, all images and masks can be held in NumPy arrays. The paths are shuffled with the same seed so pairs stay aligned, every file is resized to 200 × 200, and mask labels are shifted from 1–3 to 0–2.
overview.importance: These few lines decide the data contract of the whole model: input shape (200, 200, 3), target shape (200, 200, 1) with integer labels 0, 1, 2, and an image order that does not group samples by breed. Getting any of these wrong (mismatched shuffles, interpolated labels, labels starting at 1) silently ruins training.

Explain why both path lists are shuffled with random.Random(1337)

paragraphs.excerpt: Next, let’s load our inputs and targets into two NumPy arrays.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors will load all inputs and targets into two NumPy arrays, which is feasible because the dataset is very small.
paragraphs.what_it_means: About 7,390 images (p.335) at 200 × 200 × 3 float32 values take roughly 7,390 × 120,000 × 4 bytes ≈ 3.5 GB, and the uint8 masks take about 0.3 GB. That fits in the RAM of a typical workstation or Colab instance, so no streaming pipeline (tf.data, generators) is needed. (The memory estimate is our own arithmetic, not stated in the book.)
paragraphs.why_it_matters: In-memory arrays make the code simple: you can index, slice into train/validation (p.338) and pass arrays directly to model.fit. For larger datasets you would use a data pipeline instead, as in chapter 8's image_dataset_from_directory.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Trade-off between simplicity (arrays in RAM) and scalability (streamed datasets).

terminology.meaning: Argument of load_img that resizes the image to (height, width) on load; by default with nearest-neighbour interpolation.
Shuffling with a random generator initialized from a fixed seed, so the permutation is reproducible.

concepts.name: Segmentation mask
concepts.definition: A single-channel image whose integer values give the class of each pixel of the input.
concepts.intuition: Figure 11.4 is a map of the photo with three colours: pet, background, outline.
concepts.technical: After path_to_target, each mask is a uint8 array of shape (200, 200, 1) with values in {0, 1, 2}.
concepts.significance: The per-pixel target for the model's 3-way softmax output.
concepts.example: A pixel on the cat's back: 0; on the carpet: 1; on the yellow outline band: 2.
concepts.misconception: The colours in figure 11.4 are not stored in the file; they come from the display colormap.

concepts.name: Aligned shuffling of paired lists
concepts.definition: Applying the same random permutation to two lists that must stay in correspondence.
concepts.intuition: Shuffle two decks of cards in exactly the same way so card k of one deck still matches card k of the other.
concepts.technical: random.Random(1337) creates an independent generator; two generators with the same seed produce the same sequence, so shuffle() on equal-length lists yields the same permutation.
concepts.significance: Breaks the breed-sorted order (otherwise the last 1,000 validation samples on p.338 would all be a few breeds) without breaking image-mask pairing.
concepts.example: If input_img_paths[0] is Abyssinian_1.jpg and target_paths[0] is Abyssinian_1.png, after both shuffles they end up at the same new index.
concepts.misconception: Calling random.shuffle twice on the global generator would NOT work: the second call continues the random stream and gives a different permutation.

concepts.name: Zero-based integer class labels
concepts.definition: Class ids encoded as integers 0..K-1, as expected by sparse categorical cross-entropy.
concepts.intuition: Labels are array indices into the model's output probability vector, so they must start at 0.
concepts.technical: img.astype("uint8") - 1 maps {1, 2, 3} to {0, 1, 2}; with num_classes=3 the softmax has 3 entries indexed 0, 1, 2.
concepts.significance: A label 3 with only 3 output classes would be out of range and cause an error or wrong loss.
concepts.example: Contour pixels: 3 → 2, the index of the third softmax output.
concepts.misconception: Shifting the labels does not change their meaning, only their encoding.

math.title: Label shift for training targets

variables.meaning: Original trimap label at pixel (i, j): 1 foreground, 2 background, 3 contour

math.operations: Elementwise subtraction on a uint8 array.
math.purpose: Make labels valid indices for a 3-class softmax / sparse cross-entropy.
math.intuition: Shift the label scale so it starts at zero.

code.title: Shuffling paths and defining image/mask loaders
code.original_code:
import numpy as np
import random

img_size = (200, 200)
num_imgs = len(input_img_paths)

random.Random(1337).shuffle(input_img_paths)
random.Random(1337).shuffle(target_paths)

def path_to_input_image(path):
    return img_to_array(load_img(path, target_size=img_size))

def path_to_target(path):
    img = img_to_array(
        load_img(path, target_size=img_size, color_mode="grayscale")
    )
    img = img.astype("uint8") - 1
    return img
code.what_it_does: Fixes the working image size, counts samples, shuffles both path lists identically, and defines functions that turn a path into a (200, 200, 3) float32 image array or a (200, 200, 1) uint8 label array with labels 0–2. The block continues on p.338 with the loop that allocates and fills the arrays.

line_explanations.explanation: NumPy for arrays; Python's random module for shuffling.
Callout: 'We resize everything to 200 x 200 for this example.'
Callout: 'Total number of samples in the data.'
Callout: shuffles the file paths (originally sorted by breed); the same seed 1337 in both statements keeps input and target paths in the same order. shuffle works in place.
Loads an RGB image resized to 200 × 200 and converts it to a float32 array (200, 200, 3) with values 0–255.
Loads the mask resized to 200 × 200 with a single channel → float32 (200, 200, 1).
Callout: 'Subtracts 1 so that our labels become 0, 1, and 2.' The cast to uint8 also reduces memory 4×.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: the path lists from p.335. Outputs: shuffled lists in place and two converter functions.
code.algorithm: Fix shape → seeded aligned shuffle → per-file load/resize/convert.
code.theory_link: Supervised learning needs aligned (input, target) pairs; a random split (p.338) needs a shuffled order.

parameters.name: img_size
parameters.role: Target spatial size (200, 200) for all inputs and masks; also the model's input size (p.338).

pitfalls: Shuffling with the global random.shuffle twice would misalign inputs and masks.

Resizing masks with a smoothing interpolation (e.g. bilinear) would create non-integer, meaningless labels; load_img's default interpolation is nearest-neighbour, which keeps labels in {1, 2, 3}. (Beyond the book.)
Resizing to a square 200 × 200 distorts aspect ratios; this is accepted for simplicity.
num_imgs is computed before shuffling, which is fine because shuffling does not change the length.

for a, b in zip(input_img_paths[:5], target_paths[:5]):
    assert os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(a))[0] == os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(b))[0]

deeper.title: Why shuffle before slicing off a validation set?
deeper.body:
Beyond the book's one-line callout:

1. The path lists were built with `sorted(...)` on p.335, so files appear alphabetically: all Abyssinians, then all Bengals, and so on.
2. On p.338 the last 1,000 samples become the validation set.
3. Without shuffling, those 1,000 would be the last few breeds alphabetically (cats and dogs whose names start with late letters), so the validation set would not represent the training distribution.
4. Shuffling with a fixed seed makes the split random yet reproducible from run to run.

deeper.title: Memory budget of in-memory loading
deeper.body: Our own estimate (not in the book): inputs `7390 × 200 × 200 × 3 × 4 bytes ≈ 3.55 GB` (float32), targets `7390 × 200 × 200 × 1 × 1 byte ≈ 0.30 GB` (uint8). Storing the inputs as uint8 and rescaling in the model (the `Rescaling(1/255)` layer on p.338) could cut input memory 4×.

misconceptions.claim: Using random.shuffle on both lists keeps them aligned.
misconceptions.correction: Only if both shuffles use generators in the same state; the book creates a fresh random.Random(1337) for each list for exactly this reason.

misconceptions.claim: The purple/teal/yellow colours are the mask's stored values.
misconceptions.correction: The mask stores 1, 2, 3; the colours come from rescaling for display (p.336) plus Matplotlib's default colormap.

misconceptions.claim: Labels must be shifted because uint8 cannot hold 3.
misconceptions.correction: uint8 holds 0–255; the shift is needed because class indices for a 3-class softmax must be 0, 1, 2.

takeaways: Figure 11.4 shows the trimap: pet, background and a thick contour band.
The dataset is small enough to load fully into RAM as NumPy arrays.
Two random.Random(1337) generators shuffle inputs and masks identically, breaking the breed order without breaking pairs.
Mask labels are shifted to 0, 1, 2 so they are valid class indices.

questions.question: Why does the code create a new random.Random(1337) for each shuffle?
options: So both lists receive the same permutation and stay aligned
To shuffle the masks differently from the images
questions.answer: So both lists receive the same permutation and stay aligned
questions.explanation: The callout says the same seed keeps input and target paths in the same order. Speed is irrelevant, random.shuffle works on any list, and shuffling them differently would destroy the pairing.

questions.question: Why were the paths shuffled at all?
questions.answer: They were originally sorted by breed; shuffling ensures the later train/validation split is random rather than breed-based.
questions.explanation: Callout plus the split on p.338, which takes the last 1,000 samples.

questions.question: What shape and dtype does path_to_target return?
questions.answer: A uint8 array of shape (200, 200, 1) with values 0, 1, 2.
questions.explanation: Grayscale load at img_size gives one channel; astype("uint8") - 1 sets dtype and shifts labels.

questions.question: Why must the labels start at 0 rather than 1?
questions.answer: Because they index the model's per-pixel softmax output with num_classes=3 entries (indices 0, 1, 2); sparse cross-entropy uses the label as an index.
questions.explanation: With labels 1–3, label 3 would be out of range.

questions.question: A mask row reads [3, 1, 1, 2]. What does path_to_target turn it into?
In figure 11.4, which colour corresponds to the contour class, and why does it appear as a thick band?
questions.answer: Yellow (highest value, 254). The contour class marks the uncertain boundary region around the pet, which annotators drew as a band several pixels wide.
questions.explanation: Viridis maps the largest value to yellow; the contour is label 3, the highest.

questions.question: Could you rewrite the alignment-preserving shuffle using a single NumPy permutation applied to both lists?
questions.answer: Yes: perm = np.random.default_rng(1337).permutation(n); then index both lists with perm.
questions.explanation: Any method that applies one permutation to both lists preserves pairing.
